structure.form: letter collection with substantial editorial framing narrative by the recipient, organized into labeled thematic sections

characters.name: Linda Levy (Linda Castellani)
characters.note: One of the women Dick described among his 'dark-haired girls'; compiled and annotated this collection of their correspondence in 2008, framing it explicitly as a personal account meant to precede public perceptions being fixed by an in-development biopic.

motifs: The recurring 'dark-haired girl' figure across Dick's life and fiction, here documented from one specific real correspondent's own perspective
A recipient's personal account offered explicitly as a counterweight to a forthcoming dramatized public portrayal
Physical ephemera (photographs, signed prints, a purchased magazine) presented alongside the letters as evidence of a lived relationship
reading.significance: This self-published collection is a valuable, if non-scholarly, primary-source window into one of Dick's real-life romantic entanglements with the recurring 'dark-haired girl' figure that appears throughout his fiction and his own self-mythologizing correspondence (notably his December 1972 letter to Roger Zelazny). Because it is compiled and framed entirely by the recipient rather than through independent editorial verification, its characterizations of Dick -- both sympathetic and critical -- should be read as one participant's testimony rather than as adjudicated biographical fact.
reading.closing_note: Castellani's explicit motive for publishing -- getting her account into print before a Paul Giamatti biopic then in development could fix a different public image of Dick -- frames the entire collection as an act of personal historical intervention as much as archival preservation.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

critical_caution: This is a fan-compiled and self-published memoir/letters collection by Linda Levy (writing as Linda Castellani), not a scholarly or major-press edition. Its framing of Dick's character, including claims about violence toward women, is Castellani's own account and should be read as one participant's testimony rather than adjudicated fact.
